text.p: Not many people at Roland Garros were afraid of Filip Dewulf before this French Open and even the Belgian never dreamt he would be snapping at the heels of John McEnroe by the end of the first week.

The qualifier's days of catching opponents unawares, though, are probably over after a stunning 5-7 6-1 6-4 7-5 win over clay specialist Alex Corretja which guaranteed Belgium their first player in a Grand Slam quarter-final in the Open era.

If Dewulf can go one better in the last eight against Sweden's Magnus Norman, he will emulate McEnroe's famous achievement in 1977 when the American burst out of the rose gardens at the Wimbledon qualifying tournament in Roehampton to reach the semifinals at the All England Club.

No qualifier has managed it at any Grand Slam since, but the 25-year-old son of a Belgian pharmacist has already gone a long way towards remedying a sketchy record at major events where he has never previously ventured beyond the second round.

"I'll pick up a newspaper tomorrow just to see the result with my own eyes," grinned Dewulf, ranked 122 in the world. "I came here to play the qualifying and now I'm in the quarter-finals. It's totally unexpected."

As the blissful sunshine of the opening week gave way to chilly winds and swirling clouds of dust on Sunday, the big, bad forehand which Dewulf is not shy about using proved fatal for a harassed Corretja, seeded eighth but regarded as a leading contender for the French title.
The Spaniard saved two match points before scrambling back to 5-5 in the final set, only to weaken his own position with a display of sportsmanship in the crucial next game.
A Dewulf approach was called out by the line-judge, but Corretja overruled the decision and, when it was replayed, the Spaniard was rewarded for his efforts by going 6-5 down.

"If I see the ball on the line, I have to be honest whether it's break point or advantage to him or whatever," said Corretja, whose frustration had been apparent much earlier when he threw back his head and howled at the heavens in Catalan after one woeful mis-hit.
"That wasn't the reason he won, he just played better than me. The wind killed my game today. It was one of the worst matches of my life."
Dewulf has received plenty of support from both the Belgian and French public during his momentous week in Paris which has included two successive five-set wins before he ran into Corretja.
This may not last as Belgium are due to face France in a Davis Cup World Group play-off in September, but for Dewulf is living only for the present.
"When I won the second set I started to realise I could win the match because although he was very much the man in form on clay courts, he had a lot of problems with the wind.
"Now I've nothing to lose. I hope I'll go on the court in two days time in the same frame of mind and play well." The Dewulf man is not dead yet.
